meta.note: Coordinates marked confidence=approximate are rounded to the site area, not an exact address. Many sites are private property, structurally unsafe or actively patrolled. This dataset documents them; it is not an invitation to enter.
meta.accessNote: Access ratings are an assessment from each site’s ownership, status and press coverage — they are not verified on the ground and they change. "No known security" is not permission: entering private property without it is trespass, and many of these buildings are structurally unsafe regardless of who is watching.
meta.scope: Only places that are actually abandoned. Buildings still in everyday use are not listed, even when they have been damaged, and neither are sites that have been demolished away to nothing. Where part of a site has been converted and is lived in, the entry says so.

sites.name: Ayr Station Hotel
sites.summary: B-listed 1880s railway hotel, empty for years. Fire in May 2023, then a major blaze on 25 September 2023 that closed Ayr station and the rail line. South Ayrshire Council carried out emergency partial demolition; the owner's attempt to block it failed in 2024. The remaining shell is still unresolved.
sites.sourceName: Wikipedia — Ayr Station Hotel fire
sites.accessNote: Council-controlled demolition site with a standing cordon around the shell.

sites.name: Sauchiehall Street derelict block
sites.summary: Three-storey derelict building in Glasgow city centre went up around 01:36 on Tuesday 1 September 2026. Nine appliances, one height appliance and three specialist resources attended. Roads closed, no injuries reported.
sites.sourceName: Scottish Fire and Rescue Service
sites.accessNote: Recent fire scene: hoardings, cordon and contractor security.

sites.name: Princes Street disused building
sites.summary: A large fire engulfed a disused building on Princes Street in the early hours of 9 July 2026. The site was earmarked for hotel conversion. Transport across central Edinburgh was disrupted for days.
sites.sourceName: Bloomberg
sites.accessNote: Recent fire scene on a main city street, cordoned and watched.

sites.name: Union Corner, Union Street
sites.summary: Major fire on 8 March 2026 in the Union Corner building at Union Street and Gordon Street in central Glasgow, a long-vacant commercial block near Central Station.
sites.sourceName: Wikipedia — Union Street fire
sites.accessNote: Recent fire scene, hoarded and cordoned in the city centre.

sites.name: Strathmartine Hospital
sites.summary: Former psychiatric hospital closed in 2003. The site has become one of Dundee's worst hotspots for deliberate fire-raising, with repeated blazes across the abandoned wards over two decades.
sites.sourceName: Scottish Fire and Rescue Service
sites.accessNote: Known arson hotspot, so the site is watched and reported on.

sites.name: Bangour Village Hospital
sites.summary: Edwardian 'colony plan' psychiatric hospital opened 1906 — dozens of separate villas, a church and its own railway. Closed 2004 and left to rot; probably Scotland's best-known urbex site. Fire and vandalism have hit several villas.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland
sites.accessNote: Site security during redevelopment; the best-known urbex target in Scotland, so it is actively watched.

sites.name: Hartwood Hospital
sites.summary: Once the largest mental asylum in Europe with around 2,500 patients. Closed in the late 1990s, partially burned down and now severely unstable — collapsed floors and open roofs throughout the twin-towered main block.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland
sites.accessNote: Fenced. Collapsed floors and open shafts make it one of the most dangerous ruins in the country.

sites.name: St Peter's Seminary, Cardross
sites.summary: Brutalist Category A-listed seminary by Gillespie, Kidd & Coia, opened 1966, abandoned by 1987. Repeatedly vandalised and burned. Widely called Scotland's most important modern ruin; multiple restoration schemes have failed.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland
sites.accessNote: The Kilmahew woodland around it is walkable, but the building itself is fenced off.

sites.name: Gartloch Hospital
sites.status: Hospital core derelict, estate is housing
sites.summary: Victorian asylum with a distinctive clock tower, closed 1996. The land around it was built out as housing and people live there now; the listed hospital core itself stayed empty, was gutted by fire and remains a shell behind hoardings.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland
sites.partlyOccupied: The former estate around it is a lived-in housing development.

sites.name: Lennox Castle Hospital
sites.summary: 1837 castle that became a hospital for people with learning disabilities, closed 2002. Gutted by fire in 2008 and again since. The roofless shell sits behind the Celtic FC training ground.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland

sites.name: Woodilee Hospital
sites.status: Listed fragments derelict, rest is housing
sites.summary: Barony Parochial Asylum, opened 1875, closed 2000. Almost all of it has been cleared and replaced by housing that is lived in today — what is left on the map here is the handful of listed buildings that were never converted and are still empty and decaying.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland
sites.partlyOccupied: Most of the site is an occupied housing estate.

sites.name: Sunnyside Royal Hospital
sites.summary: Scotland's first purpose-built asylum (founded 1781, this site from 1858), closed 2011. Large listed complex near Montrose, vacant and on the at-risk register while conversion plans stall.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland

sites.name: Craig Dunain Hospital
sites.summary: Inverness District Asylum, opened 1864, closed 2000. Part of the complex was converted into flats that are lived in; the section wrecked by a major fire while the building stood empty was never rebuilt and is still a burnt-out ruin.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland
sites.partlyOccupied: The converted blocks are occupied flats.

sites.name: Argyll and Bute Hospital, Lochgilphead
sites.summary: The last of Scotland's Victorian psychiatric asylums still in use, finally closed in 2017. Now a listed building awaiting a future.
sites.sourceName: Carte Urbex

sites.name: Mavisbank House
sites.summary: Category A-listed 1720s Palladian villa by William Adam, gutted by fire in 1973 and left open to the sky for fifty years. A long-running poster child for the Buildings at Risk Register; a rescue project finally started in the 2020s.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland
sites.accessNote: Active conservation project — scaffolded working site.

sites.name: Cambusnethan Priory
sites.summary: 1820 Gothic Revival mansion near Wishaw, a hotel and then a medieval-banquet venue before fires in the 1980s left it roofless. Category B-listed and among the most-photographed derelicts in Lanarkshire.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland

sites.name: Crawford Priory
sites.summary: Extravagant Gothic country house near Cupar, abandoned since the 1970s. Roof gone, walls progressively collapsing; sections have come down in recent storms.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland
sites.accessNote: Private estate. Masonry has come down in recent storms.

sites.name: Buchanan Castle
sites.summary: Seat of the Dukes of Montrose, a WWII military hospital (Rudolf Hess was treated here), then stripped of its roof in 1954 to avoid tax. The shell has stood open ever since.
sites.sourceName: Travels with a Kilt

sites.name: Dunmore Park House
sites.summary: 1820s Tudor-Gothic mansion near Airth, abandoned and unroofed since the 1960s–70s. Next to the famous Dunmore Pineapple. Steadily losing masonry.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland

sites.name: Dunalastair House
sites.summary: Baronial mansion near Kinloch Rannoch, used to billet Polish troops in WWII and derelict ever since. Now a genuinely dangerous ruin with collapsing floors.
sites.sourceName: Travels with a Kilt
sites.accessNote: Private land, and genuinely dangerous — floors have gone.

sites.name: Broadford Works
sites.summary: Category A-listed linen mill complex, one of the oldest surviving iron-framed mills in Britain. Closed 2004, hit by fire while vacant and repeatedly broken into as redevelopment plans drag on.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland

sites.name: Glenmavis Distillery
sites.summary: Bathgate distillery closed in the early 20th century. Surviving listed ranges are roofless and overgrown, long-standing entries on the at-risk register.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland

sites.name: Arichonan Township
sites.summary: Abandoned after the 1848 clearance, when residents resisted eviction and were tried in Inveraray. Stone walls and gables still stand on the hillside above Loch Sween.
sites.sourceName: Travels with a Kilt

sites.name: Badbea Clearance Village
sites.summary: Cliff-top settlement on the Caithness coast built by families cleared from inland straths. Conditions were so exposed that children and livestock were reportedly tethered. Last resident left in 1911.
sites.sourceName: Travelness

sites.name: Kilchurn Castle
sites.summary: 15th-century Campbell stronghold on Loch Awe, damaged by lightning in the 1760s and abandoned. Now in state care — the one entry here you can visit legally and safely.
sites.sourceName: Historic Environment Scotland
sites.accessNote: In state care. Open seasonally — the one site here you can simply walk into.

sites.name: Fearn Airfield
sites.summary: Scotland’s single largest vacant and derelict site at 386 hectares. Built in 1941 as an RAF airfield and later a Royal Navy air station, it has been derelict for at least four decades — runways, dispersals and hangar bases still readable from the air.
sites.sourceName: The Ferret — largest vacant and derelict sites in Scotland
sites.accessNote: Working farmland over most of the 386 ha.

sites.name: Fendom Airfield, Tain
sites.summary: RAF weapons range and wartime airfield opened in 1941 on the Dornoch Firth. Derelict by 1980 at the latest; 295 hectares of it, making it the third-largest derelict site in the country.
sites.sourceName: The Ferret — largest vacant and derelict sites in Scotland
sites.accessNote: Farmland and MOD range land adjoin the site.

sites.name: Baldoon Airfield (RAF Wigtown)
sites.summary: RAF Wigtown closed in 1948 and has been left alone ever since. As recently as 2017 the site still held its control towers, hangars, two runways and fourteen abandoned air raid shelters across 184 hectares.
sites.sourceName: The Ferret — largest vacant and derelict sites in Scotland
sites.accessNote: Farmland; the surviving structures are on private ground.

sites.name: Edzell Airbase
sites.status: Airfield derelict, part is an industrial estate
sites.summary: A WWI airfield that became RAF Edzell and then a US Navy Cold War listening station with a huge circular antenna array. The Americans left in 1997. A corner of it now trades as an industrial estate; the runways, bunkers and abandoned base buildings across the remaining 170 hectares do not.
sites.sourceName: The Ferret — largest vacant and derelict sites in Scotland
sites.accessNote: Part of the site is now a working industrial estate.
sites.partlyOccupied: Part of the site is a working industrial estate.

sites.name: RAF Machrihanish
sites.status: Base buildings derelict, airfield still operational
sites.summary: NATO forward base on the Kintyre peninsula with one of the longest runways in Europe, built to take heavy transports and rumoured to have hosted US special forces. The RAF left in 1997. The runway is still flown from and part of the site trades as a business park, but the hardened shelters, bunkers and accommodation blocks are abandoned.
sites.sourceName: Wikipedia
sites.accessNote: The airfield is still operational and MOD land adjoins it.
sites.partlyOccupied: The runway and a business park are in use; MOD land adjoins.

sites.name: RAF Aird Uig / Gallan Head
sites.summary: Cold War radar station on the westernmost headland of Lewis, decommissioned in 1958 and progressively abandoned. Empty accommodation blocks and radar platforms sit above the cliffs; the headland has since passed to a community trust.
sites.sourceName: Gary Gough — RAF Aird Uig
sites.accessNote: The headland is community-owned with public access; the buildings themselves are not maintained.

sites.name: RAF Milltown
sites.summary: Airfield north-east of Elgin on the Moray Firth. Flying stopped in 1977 and it carried on as a communications station before winding down; runways, dispersals and antenna bases remain across the flat coastal ground.
sites.sourceName: Wikipedia

sites.name: Ardeer Explosives Works
sites.summary: Alfred Nobel opened his dynamite factory on the Ardeer sands in 1871 — at its peak the largest explosives works in the world, with thousands of staff and its own railway. A small operational plant survives at one end; the other 331 hectares of blast mounds, blockhouses and buried magazines have been derelict since 2005.
sites.sourceName: The Ferret — largest vacant and derelict sites in Scotland
sites.accessNote: Parts of the wider site are still operational chemical works with real security.
sites.partlyOccupied: Parts of the wider site are still a working chemical plant.

sites.name: Bogside, Irvine
sites.summary: The other half of the Nobel Industries empire on the Ayrshire coast, plus a former racecourse. Derelict since 2005 and, at 221 hectares, the sixth-largest abandoned site in Scotland.
sites.sourceName: The Ferret — largest vacant and derelict sites in Scotland

sites.name: Port of Ardersier
sites.status: Yard derelict, port redevelopment under way
sites.summary: Oil-platform fabrication yard opened in the early 1970s on the Moray Firth, employing thousands through the North Sea boom. Closed in 2001 and empty for two decades; work has since started on turning it into an operational port, so parts of the 254-hectare site are a live construction project rather than a ruin.
sites.sourceName: The Ferret — largest vacant and derelict sites in Scotland
sites.accessNote: Being redeveloped as an operational port; manned security.
sites.partlyOccupied: An active port redevelopment with staff on site.

sites.name: Powharnel opencast mine, Muirkirk
sites.summary: Opencast coal mine abandoned in 2013 when Scottish Coal went into liquidation, leaving the restoration bond nowhere near enough to fill the void. 245 hectares of unrestored workings — one of the scandals of the Ayrshire coalfield.
sites.sourceName: The Ferret — largest vacant and derelict sites in Scotland
sites.accessNote: Open moorland, but unrestored opencast voids and flooded pits.

sites.name: Benbain opencast mine
sites.summary: Another East Ayrshire opencast left unfinished by the 2013 collapse of Scottish Coal. 193 hectares of spoil and open void that were supposed to be returned to farmland.
sites.sourceName: The Ferret — largest vacant and derelict sites in Scotland
sites.accessNote: Open moorland with unrestored opencast voids.

sites.name: Strathmore railway line
sites.summary: The old main line through Strathmore, closed to passengers in 1967 under the Beeching cuts and to freight in the early 1980s. 165 hectares of abandoned trackbed, cuttings, bridges and shuttered station buildings.
sites.sourceName: The Ferret — largest vacant and derelict sites in Scotland

sites.name: Hirta, St Kilda
sites.summary: Britain’s most remote inhabited place until the 36 remaining islanders asked to be taken off. On 29 August 1930 the Harebell carried them to the mainland, ending over 2,000 years of habitation. They left a plate of oats and an open Bible in each cottage. Now a double UNESCO World Heritage Site.
sites.sourceName: Wikipedia — Hirta
sites.accessNote: National Trust for Scotland. Landing is possible by boat in summer, subject to their rules.

sites.name: Mingulay
sites.summary: Island at the southern tip of the Outer Hebrides where around 30 families lived by crofting, fishing and fowling on 200-metre sea cliffs. Conditions and isolation beat them and the last left in 1912. The village street of roofless houses still stands above the bay.
sites.sourceName: Wikipedia — Mingulay
sites.accessNote: National Trust for Scotland; landing by boat, weather permitting.

sites.name: Swona
sites.summary: From the early 1930s a single family, the Rosies, were the only people on this Pentland Firth island. In 1974 the last brother and sister sailed off, leaving the house and their cattle behind. The cattle were never collected and their descendants still run wild there — a feral herd studied by scientists.
sites.sourceName: Wikipedia — Swona
sites.accessNote: Privately owned island with a feral cattle herd. No landing without permission.

sites.name: Stroma
sites.summary: Island in the Pentland Firth whose population peaked at around 375 in the early 1900s. As families left, the school, shop and ferry became unviable and the community collapsed; the last residents went in 1962. A harbour finished just as the island emptied is still there.
sites.sourceName: The Scotsman — Nine abandoned islands of Scotland
sites.accessNote: Privately owned but access is not obstructed; boat landing only.

sites.name: Inchkeith
sites.summary: Fortress island in the middle of the Firth of Forth, fortified from the 16th century and heavily built up with gun batteries and barracks in both World Wars. The garrison left after 1945 and the lighthouse was automated in 1986; the tunnels, emplacements and empty blocks have been derelict ever since.
sites.sourceName: The Sunday Post
sites.accessNote: Privately owned island. Tunnels and gun emplacements are unlit and unmaintained.

sites.name: Hallaig, Raasay
sites.summary: Township on the east side of Raasay cleared in the 1850s, its people shipped to Australia. Immortalised in Sorley MacLean’s poem "Hallaig", probably the best-known Gaelic poem of the 20th century. Only stone footings and a memorial cairn remain.
sites.sourceName: Travelness

sites.name: Rosal Township, Strathnaver
sites.summary: One of the townships burned out in the Sutherland Clearances of 1814 by Patrick Sellar’s men. Excavated in the 1960s and now an interpreted trail in Strathnaver — the clearest surviving plan of a pre-Clearance Highland settlement.
sites.sourceName: Historic Environment Scotland
sites.accessNote: Interpreted trail on Forestry and Land Scotland ground.

sites.name: Tureen Street School
sites.summary: Yellow ashlar board school in Calton, finished in 1875 and one of the oldest surviving school buildings in Glasgow. Long closed, windows boarded, and listed on the Buildings at Risk Register while conversion schemes come and go.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland
sites.accessNote: Boarded and monitored while conversion schemes are considered.

sites.name: Holmlea Primary School
sites.summary: Edwardian red sandstone board school in Cathcart, closed in the 2000s and left empty. Repeatedly broken into and vandalised while housing conversion plans stalled.
sites.sourceName: Wikipedia

sites.name: Fern School
sites.summary: Late-19th-century rural primary school. Funding cuts in the 1990s cut rolls until it closed in the mid-2000s; it has stood empty ever since, with desks, books and coat pegs still in place — a well-known urbex time capsule.
sites.sourceName: Obsidian Urbex Photography
sites.accessNote: Private rural property; no known active security, which is why the interior survived.

sites.name: Former Inverkeithing Primary School
sites.summary: The town’s old primary school stood empty after pupils moved to a new building, and was gutted by a large fire that brought Scottish Fire and Rescue crews out in force — the classic fate of a vacant Scottish school.
sites.sourceName: Scottish Fire and Rescue Service

sites.name: Tirfergus House
sites.summary: Kintyre country house near Campbeltown, abandoned in the second half of the 20th century and now a roofless shell being taken apart by weather and vegetation.
sites.sourceName: Wikipedia

sites.name: Rosslynlee Hospital
sites.summary: Midlothian District Asylum of 1874, latterly a psychiatric hospital, closed around 2011. The listed main block with its tower has stood empty and open to the weather since, with periodic vandalism and small fires.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland

sites.name: Kingseat Hospital
sites.status: Admin block and villas derelict, rest converted
sites.summary: Aberdeen District Asylum, built on the same villa-colony plan as Bangour and opened in 1904, closed in the mid-1990s. Some villas became private houses and are occupied; the administration block and the villas nobody bought were left to rot and burn.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland
sites.partlyOccupied: Several villas are now private homes.
